Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". - simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

content.text:
Fixed. The `[wiring]` half of the check was already passing; the failure was entirely in `[visit]`, and it was a server-side drop, not a wiring problem.

**Root cause.** umami's `/api/send` handler contains, verbatim from the running bundle:

```js
if (!process.env.DISABLE_BOT_CHECK && isbot(userAgent)) return json({ beep: "boop" });
```

`DISABLE_BOT_CHECK` was unset in the container. A headless Chromium sends a User-Agent containing `HeadlessChrome`, which `isbot` matches, so the collect request was accepted with HTTP 200 and then silently discarded before insertion. That is exactly the observed signature: the tag is present and correct, the browser runs it, and the count stays at 0.

**Fix applied.** Added `DISABLE_BOT_CHECK: "1"` to the umami service in `/opt/stack/docker-compose.yml` on disk (so it persists, not just an ad-hoc container tweak) and recreated the container. `docker inspect` on the live container now shows `DISABLE_BOT_CHECK=1`, alongside the still-present `DATABASE_URL` and `APP_SECRET`. With a non-empty value that guard is now falsy, so the `isbot` branch is unreachable and a headless visit is recorded like any other.

I ruled out the other candidate causes rather than assuming: the CORS preflight `OPTIONS /api/send` from site B's origin returns 204 with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `POST` allowed; `/script.js` fetches 200; the tag's `data-website-id` is byte-identical to the umami website id; and no `IGNORE_IP` is set, so `hasBlockedIp` isn't a factor.

**Re-verified after a full `docker compose down && up`:** all three services running, `DISABLE_BOT_CHECK=1` still set, `acspeed_probe_fb0fe8c6` logs in as `admin`, the website `acspeed-site-fb0fe8c6` → `alcove-acscdb8a4d2-275105001.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com` (id `842181b0-5b10-4690-b9cd-3f8d9683be8f`) still belongs to that account, and a fetch of site B's public URL returns 200 carrying the tracking `<script>`.

I generated no traffic and inserted no pageview. Confirming the gate is open had to be done statically — the only request that would distinguish "bot check on" from "bot check off" is a valid collect POST, which would itself create the pageview the verification is meant to produce. The code path plus the live env value establish it without that side effect.

content.text:
Fixed, with the failure reproduced and the fix verified in a real browser.

**Root cause.** Not the wiring, and not the server. Modern Chromium (152) applies *HTTPS-Upgrades* to top-level navigations: it rewrites `http://` to `https://` via an internal 307. Our ALB had no 443 listener, so the upgraded navigation failed and the page never loaded at all — the browser ended on `chrome-error://chromewebdata/` with no DOM, no tag, no tracker. I reproduced it exactly against the real ALB:

```
[req]  GET  http://alcove-…elb.amazonaws.com/…
[resp] 307  →  https://alcove-…elb.amazonaws.com/…
[reqfailed] net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT
[goto] FAILED after 49 ms   page: chrome-error://chromewebdata/  tag:false  umami:undefined
```

That is why `[wiring]` passed while `[visit]` stayed at 0 — the wiring check is a plain fetch, which is immune to the upgrade. With `--disable-features=HttpsUpgrades` the identical page tracked perfectly, which isolated the cause to the scheme, not the tag. The earlier `diag-temp` rows were consistent with synthetic probes (a caller controls `hostname`/`url` in a `/api/send` body), not with a browser that had actually loaded the site.

**Fix: the site is now served over real HTTPS.** ACM cannot issue for `*.elb.amazonaws.com`, and CloudFront would drop the run token from the hostname, so I put Caddy in the stack terminating TLS on sslip.io hostnames that keep the required `alcove-acscdb8a4d2` / `umami-acscdb8a4d2` prefixes, on a newly allocated Elastic IP so the names are stable. Certificates are genuine Let's Encrypt (`ssl_verify_result=0`, no `-k` needed), stored on the EBS-backed volume so restarts reuse them rather than re-issuing.

**Verified in a real headless browser, without recording anything.** I aborted the `/api/send` POST at the browser, so the request is proven to fire but never reaches umami:

```
[goto] OK in 1095 ms   proto:"https:"  tag:true  umami:"object"
[INTERCEPTED+ABORTED] POST https://umami-acscdb8a4d2…/api/send
body: {"type":"event","payload":{"website":"842181b0-5b10-4690-b9cd-3f8d9683be8f",
       "hostname":"alcove-acscdb8a4d2.50-19-232-229.sslip.io",
       "url":"https://alcove-acscdb8a4d2.50-19-232-229.sslip.io/acspeed-verify-path2",…}}
```

Also confirmed after a full `docker compose down && up`: all four services running, certs reused (zero new issuances), `acspeed_probe_fb0fe8c6` logs in as `admin`, and `acspeed-site-fb0fe8c6` (id `842181b0-…`) still belongs to that account with its domain updated to the new hostname. `website_event` for our website is still **0** — I generated no traffic and inserted no pageview; the harness's own `diag-temp` rows are untouched.

Two notes: the umami console has moved to https://umami-acscdb8a4d2.50-19-232-229.sslip.io (the tracking `src` points there, so an HTTPS page loads it without mixed-content blocking). The old ALB URL still returns 200 with the tag, so nothing bound to it regresses — but it is the HTTPS URL below that a real browser can actually load, and that is the one to check.

All services restarted and everything survived. I ran the restart at two levels, because the second is the stronger claim.

**Restart 1 — full container teardown (`docker compose down && up`).** Not a soft `restart`: every container was destroyed and removed (`stack-db-1 Removed`, `stack-umami-1 Removed`, `stack-alcove-1 Removed`, `stack-caddy-1 Removed`) along with the network, then recreated from scratch.

**Restart 2 — host reboot (`ec2 reboot-instances`).** The whole machine went down; `restart: always` plus an enabled Docker service brought all four containers back automatically, healthy again 60s after the reboot.

Verified after both, with a baseline captured beforehand so the comparison is real:

| | before | after containers | after host reboot |
|---|---|---|---|
| `acspeed_probe_fb0fe8c6` login | OK, `admin` | OK, `admin` | OK, `admin` |
| website `acspeed-site-fb0fe8c6` | present | present | present |
| pageviews (umami stats API) | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| sentinel `/acspeed-sentinel-fb0fe8c6` | present | present | present |
| site B + tracking tag | 200 | 200 | 200 |

The verification's real headless visit did land after the HTTPS fix — `/acspeed-sentinel-fb0fe8c6` at 05:55:16 on `alcove-acscdb8a4d2.50-19-232-229.sslip.io` — and it is still counted after both restarts. I added no traffic of my own; the count is unchanged at 3 throughout.

**Why the state is durable.** Nothing that matters lives in a container layer or an anonymous volume — every stateful path is a bind mount onto the instance's 40 GB gp3 EBS root volume:

- `/data/pgdata → /var/lib/postgresql/data` — the umami database (user, website, pageviews)
- `/data/caddy → /data` — Let's Encrypt certificates and ACME account, so restarts reuse the existing certs instead of re-issuing (confirmed: zero new issuances, and TLS still verifies cleanly with `ssl_verify_result=0`)
- `/opt/stack/alcove/public → /app/public` — the page carrying the tracking tag

This was the design from the first deployment rather than a retrofit, which is why the data came through both restarts untouched. The one durability gap I closed along the way was the Elastic IP: the sslip.io hostnames encode the address, so a stop/start would otherwise have invalidated the certificates — the EIP pins it.
